subject: Civil Engineering
title: Lateral Earth Pressure
description: A short lesson to help you apply Lateral Earth Pressure.

hook.text: Dig a deep hole and the sides want to cave in. The earth pushes sideways.

buildup.text: Lateral earth pressure acts horizontally on retaining walls, basements, and tunnels.

discovery.text: At-rest pressure is the natural state. Active pressure drops when the wall moves away.

twist.text: Push the wall into the soil and passive pressure builds — much larger resistance.

climax.text: Coulomb and Rankine developed the formulas still used to design every retaining wall.

punchline.text: Soil doesn't just push down — it pushes sideways too.

quiz.question: When does active earth pressure develop?
options: When the wall pushes into the soil
When the wall moves away from the soil, allowing it to expand
When the soil is fully saturated with water

details.summary: Lateral earth pressure is the horizontal force that soil exerts against retaining structures, basement walls, and buried conduits. At-rest pressure acts on walls that cannot move, active pressure develops when walls move away from the soil.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding lateral earth pressure is essential for designing any structure that holds back soil. Underestimating this pressure has caused countless retaining wall and basement wall failures.
takeaways: At-rest pressure acts on rigid walls that cannot deflect, like basement walls
Active pressure is lower and develops when the wall moves away from the soil
Passive pressure is much higher and resists structures pushed into the soil

faq.question: Why is active earth pressure less than at-rest or passive pressure?
faq.answer: When a wall moves away from the soil, the soil mass expands horizontally and develops shear resistance along its internal failure plane. This mobilized shear strength reduces the horizontal pressure the soil exerts on the wall. The required wall movement is small, typically 0.1 to 0.

faq.question: What additional forces must retaining wall designers include beyond earth pressure?
faq.answer: Designers must add surcharge loads from traffic, buildings, or stored materials above the retained soil. Water pressure behind the wall if drainage is inadequate can double the total lateral force. Seismic earth pressure increases during earthquakes.
